person: Dario Mendes, 47, owns three trucks near Joliet and drives one himself. He ships small overnight parcels on two carriers: original paperwork packets to his factoring company, ELD tablets, and tire sensors. Several came late this fall. He reads English slowly and uses a phone translator, so he wants short answers. His wife keeps the books and asks about every dollar. He will not file a weak claim, because he fears it hurts his standing, and he wants only the claims that are really owed.
stated_up_front: Please, some of my overnight parcels came late in September and October. Check which ones the carrier must pay back, and tell me simple: which parcel, how much, and when I lose it.

facts.about: What he ships and why it matters
facts.truth: Signed paperwork packets to his factoring company, Prairie Capital in Tulsa, plus ELD tablets and tire sensors. A late packet delays his factoring advance.

facts.about: Wrenpost overnight packet to Prairie Capital
facts.truth: Due Tue 13 Oct by 10:30, delivered Wed 14 Oct at 11:05. The address was correct and he dropped it before the cut-off. Transportation charge $38.40, his real money.
Standard overnight ELD tablet to a fleet-supply shop in Indianapolis, due Thu 15 Oct, arrived Fri 16 Oct. Transportation charge $27.15. Fuel surcharge was extra.
Overnight parts to Memphis on 8 Oct, late because of thunderstorms. He remembers the carrier sent a weather notice. He does not want to claim it.
Box of tire sensors by Ground to Columbus, 3 days late, charge $14.90. He thinks it should be refunded, but is not sure.
ELD vendor in Atlanta. He forgot Suite 210 on the label, and the vendor wrote that it sat at their front desk.
Adult-signature packet to a small broker, Ferncastle Freight. The office was closed and nobody could sign. The broker's email confirms this.
He wrote himself a Gmail note asking for a $29.75 credit on a late overnight in early October. He believes Lanecourier already gave it.
Two late overnight parcels on the weekly invoice dated 12 Oct. One cost $41.20 and one $33.60. He wants to check their addresses.
Two parcels from mid-September were late, but he waited and thinks the time to ask has passed. Maybe about 6 October.
An email from a refund audit company offers to file claims for him and keep half. He does not want it, since a dispatch service once took 8% of his gross.

unknowns: How many days he has to claim with each carrier, or when each window starts
Which services each carrier's guarantee covers and which are suspended
Whether the carrier allows a few seconds of lateness before a parcel counts as late
Whether the carrier's weather notice is enough to refuse a claim
